name: SmartSpool for AMS 2 Pro
blurb: A screw-free RFID kit in development to help your AMS 2 Pro identify the filament you load, using reusable spool tags.

rewards.title: SmartSpool kit for one AMS 2 Pro
items: SmartSpool controller with wireless power receiver ×1
Two RFID readers with keyed cable harnesses ×1
Printable screw-free mounts and setup guide ×1
rewards.description: Build the two-reader setup for one four-bay AMS 2 Pro. Print the mounts from the included files, clip the readers onto the dividers and connect each keyed harness to the controller. Reassign the reusable tags when you change filament. Estimated delivery is late March 2027.

story_text:
Put a black PLA spool next to a black PETG spool. They look alike, but choosing the wrong material profile can spoil a print. SmartSpool started with a question from Max at Kelly Print Co. Why should the person loading a spool have to enter the same information every time?
Max is the 13-year-old designer behind SmartSpool. Kelly Print Co is based in Washington state. His dad supervises the project and runs the Kickstarter campaign. Max’s idea is to register a reusable RFID tag to a filament profile once. When a tagged spool changes bays, the goal is for its material and color to follow it in a local viewer.
What the USB prototype can do today
We attached a reusable RFID sticker to a purple spool and another to a black spool. On the bench, we connected one MFRC522 reader to an ESP32 and plugged the controller into a laptop. The USB cable powered the prototype and carried the live readings to the browser.
We saved the purple tag as “Spool 1” and the black tag as “Spool 2” in the viewer. In the first clip, Max moves the same reader from purple to black and back again. Reader A shows Spool 1, Spool 2, Spool 1, then Spool 2. The second clip gives a closer look at the screen, including “No tag in range” between reads. The spool names come from the labels we assigned to the tag IDs.
Reader A was the only reader connected for this test. The next tests are to identify which side of a divider a spool occupies, check clearance with four spools and the lid closed, and run both readers on wireless power through the AMS wall.
The prototype on our workbench
[画像: Two tagged spools, the wired RFID reader, the printed controller enclosure and the laptop running SmartSpool.]
[画像: The USB-powered controller and its reader cable beside the two tagged spools and the live activity log.]
[画像: A hand holding the MFRC522 reader above the two white RFID stickers on the spool flanges.]
[画像: The wired reader and controller on the bench with both spools and the SmartSpool browser viewer.]
How it fits
We designed two screw-free mounts for the AMS 2 Pro, one between bays 1 and 2 and one between bays 3 and 4. The planned cables run forward to differently keyed connectors. We have printed enclosures and a fit-test plate, and we are revising clearance around the reader’s wire connectors. The planned transmitter sits outside the AMS, opposite the receiver inside.
What we want to make
We’re developing a kit for one AMS 2 Pro with a controller, two reader assemblies, keyed cables, a wireless transmitter, reusable tags and printable mounts. The next controller design would put an ESP32, two reader sockets and the receiving coil on one board. We plan to prototype five boards and measure how they perform inside the machine. A local viewer for Apple, Android and the web is a later milestone.
How we’ll use the first five boards
We plan to compare each controller with the existing wireless module across the same AMS wall. We’ll record how it starts up, how warm it gets and whether voltage holds steady while both readers and Wi-Fi are active. During a separate four-spool test, we’ll log correct bay assignments, wrong assignments and reads that need a person to confirm. These results will guide the production board and the kit price.
The current firmware and build notes are available at https://github.com/KellyPrintCo/SmartSpool.
Prototype budget
Our current development estimate is $750. We’ve allowed $400 for up to two runs of five assembled controllers, $110 for ferrite, tuning parts and cable harnesses, $100 for tags and comparison reels, $80 for printed fixtures and revisions, and $60 for freight. These figures are planning allowances. We’ll price a complete kit separately using the production quantity, assembly time, testing, packaging and shipping.
risks: A reader between two spools can identify two tags without knowing which is on its left. We’ll compare the reported bay against a recorded sequence of insertions, swaps, removals and power cycles. If a read is ambiguous, our design calls for operator confirmation. We may need to change the sensing hardware before we can offer automatic four-bay assignment. Coil alignment and spacing across the AMS wall can affect available power. We’ll measure voltage and temperature while Wi-Fi and both readers are active and compare the PCB coil with the existing receiver. We’ll also check cable clearance with the lid closed and the spools shifted sideways. A board revision could change both timing and kit cost.

faq.q: Which AMS is this designed for?
faq.a: Our first target is the four-bay AMS 2 Pro. Original AMS support would require its own fit and read tests.

faq.q: How does SmartSpool know what filament is on my spool?
faq.a: You register a reusable RFID tag to a filament profile and attach it to the reel. The reader identifies the tag. When you refill a reel or move the tag, you update the material and color associated with it.

faq.q: Can it already distinguish all four bays?
faq.a: Our bench prototype recognized two different tagged spools on the same USB-connected reader. In the viewer we can confirm a bay by hand. We still need to test automatic bay assignment with two readers and four spools in the AMS 2 Pro.

faq.q: How will it mount and receive power?
faq.a: Two readers clip to the 1/2 and 3/4 dividers. Their keyed cables run to the controller at the front. The proposed kit uses a receiving coil inside the AMS and an aligned transmitter outside. We are checking fit and power delivery with all four spools loaded.

The planned status viewer targets Apple, Android and the web. Printer integration is designed around Developer Mode. The first release will document supported printers, software versions and setup steps after testing.
